### page_1
JOURNAL OF GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH, VOL. 85, NO. B7, PAGES 3523-3528, JULY 10, 1980 
Paleomagnetic Evidence for the Existence of the Geomagnetic Field 3.5 Ga Ago 
M. W. MCELHINNY AND W. E. SENANAYAKE 
Research School of Earth Sciences,/1ustralian National University, Canberra,/1. C. T. 2600,/1ustralia 
A paleomagnetic study has been made of the red dacite and pillow basalt of the Duffer Formation of 
the Pilbara craton, Australia. The dacite is currently the oldest dated rock unit in Australia, having a zir- 
con U-Pb age of 3452 + 16 Ma. Vector analysis of alternating field and thermal demagnetization results 
yield three components of magnetization. The high-temperature, high-coercivity hematite (H) com- 
ponent in the red dacite appears to be postfolding in age, as does a low-temperature, 1ow-coercivity (L) 
component observed in the pillow basalt. However, an intermediate-temperature, intermediate-coercivity 
magnetite (M) component observed in both the pillow basalt (five sites) and the red dacite (six sites) is 
clearly prefolding in age and thus older than 3.0 Ga. This M component appears to be the oldest magnet- 
ization yet recorded in paleomagnetic studies and yields a paleomagnetic pole, probably original, at 
43.9øN, 86.3øE (/195 = 7.2ø). A tentative Archaan apparent polar wander path for Australia suggests that 
the L and H components are also ancient magnetizations, probably 3.0 and 2.6 Ga old, respectively. The 
primary M component establishes the existence of the geomagnetic field at least 3.5 Ga ago. 
INTRODUCTION 
The Pilbara craton is the oldest Precambrian nucleus so far 
dated on the Australian continent. It consists basically of an 
Archaan layered succession or greenstone sequence preserved 
within several linear and arcuate belts between large oval- 
shaped granite batholiths (Figure 1). An age of 3452 + 16 Ma, 
using the U-Pb method on zircons from some volcanics near 
the base of the layered succession, is currently the oldest date 
observed on the Australian continent [Pidgeon, 1978]. The ex- 
cellent exposure of the dated volcanics and their freshness 
prompted an attempt to obtain paleomagnetic data from an 
Archaan sequence for the first time in Australia. A previous 
attempt has been made to obtain paleomagnetic data from the 
oldest dated rocks of Greenland [Fahrig and Bridgewater, 
1976]. However, an original magnetization relating to the time 
of formation of these rocks (3700 Ma) could not be deter- 
mined. The oldest preserved magnetization was apparently 
acquired during a later metamorphic event at about 2500 Ma. 
GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING 
The Archaan greenstone sequence of the Pilbara craton is 
very diverse, containing most of the rock types found in other 
greenstone sequences of the world. A detailed description of 
the succession is given by Hickman and Lipple [1975]. The 
Warrawoona Group forms the basal, predominantly volcanic 
assemblage. Relatively thin chart units occur frequently inter- 
posed between ultramafic-mafic and ultramafic-felsic cycles. 
The upper part of the succession, the Gorge Creek Group, is 
predominantly a sedimentary assemblage of banded iron for- 
mations, argillaceous rocks, and sandstones with subordinate 
pillow basalt. The layered succession commonly exceeds 15 
km in thickness and has been subjected to isoclinal folding. In 
the area sampled around Marble Bar (Figure 1) the beds are 
slightly overturned, as is clearly evidenced from the facing of 
the pillow basalts at the two localities. Greenschist facies 
metamorphism predominates in most areas. There have been 
two intervals of granite emplacement, a main one at around 
3000 Ma [Campston and/trriens, 1968] and a younger event 
when the main granite batholiths were intruded by irregular 
masses of adamellite at around 2600 Ma. The folding of the 
Archaan succession is presumed to be related to the main pe- 
riod of granite emplacement.

Columnar dacite from the Duffer Formation of the Warra- 
woona Group represents the rock type dated at 3452 Ma. It is 
a highly oxidized lava, and examination of polished sections 
shows that it is class 6 on the scale of Wilson and Watkins 
[1967]. The presence of pseudobrookite in association with ru- 
tile and hematite indicates high-temperature oxidation [Hag- 
gerty and Lindsley, 1969]. In view of the low-grade meta- 
morphism associated with these rocks the oxidation almost 
certainly took place during initial ooling. The magnetic min- 
erals have been oxidized very largely to hematite. In com- 
parison with more typical basic lavas containing relatively 
unoxidized titanomagnetites the magnetic stability of the Duf- 
fer volcanics has been greatly enhanced. This suggests that

they are ideal material for the study of the Archean of the Pil- 
bara. Their capability of withstanding greenschist meta- 
morphism should be optimized [Pullaiah et al., 1975]. 
Oriented samples were collected from the columnar dacite 
of the Duffer Formation at the locality (location I in Figure 1) 
used by Pidgeon [1978] for dating these rocks. Thirty-five sam- 
ples were collected, covering about 500 m in thickness. No 
flows can be distinguished, but they have been grouped into 
six horizons to represent separate points in time. At the pres- 
ent time the columns lie almost horizontally, the lavas being 
overturned corresponding to a dip of 101 ø toward the NE. 
Near Marble Bar, about 30 km away, rocks of the Duffer For- 
mation are also overturned corresponding to dips of 105 ø- 
110 ø in a SW direction. Twenty-three samples were collected 
from pillow basalts at five separate horizons in this region. A 
comparison of magnetization directions between the two 1o- 
calities involves a marked structural correction in applying a fold test. 
PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS 
Specimens from each sample were subjected to stepwise al- 
ternating field and thermal demagnetization, in each case in- 
volving 13 steps up to 200 mT and 640øC, respectively. The 
apparatus described by McElhinny [1966] and McElhinny et al. 
[1970] was used for these experiments, and measurements 
were made either on a Digico complete results magnetometer 
or on a Superconducting Technology two-axis cryogenic mag- 
netometer interfaced to a Digico minicomputer. The response 
of typical specimens is shown on the vector diagrams of Fig- 
ure 2. These are the so-called modified Zijderveld diagrams 
[Zijderveld, 1967], in which variations in declination and incli- 
nation are shown independently.

Fig. 4. L and H component site means observed during alternating field or thermal demagnetization. Stereographic projection of directions of magnetization are solid symbols on the lower hemisphere, open symbols on the lower hemi- sphere, and open symbols on the upper hemisphere. 
Generally, three components of magnetization were ob- 
served in both the red dacite and the pillow basalt when using 
either alternating field or thermal techniques. All samples 
usually contained a temporary component acquired during 
storage in the present geomagnetic field. In the red dacite 
there is a very resistant component preserved at fields of 200 
roT, and thermal demagnetization analysis shows that this is a 
high-temperature component with blocking temperatures 
above 525øC and up to at least 640øC. This high-temperature, 
high-coercivity component is clearly from a hematite fraction. 
In these rocks, thermal demagnetization is often difficult at 
high temperatures because of the instability of the magnetite, 
which tends to oxidize. There is also an intermediate-temper- 
ature (250ø-500øC), intermediate-coercivity (10-40 mT) com- 
ponent that appears to be derived from the magnetite fraction. 
These components will be referred to as the H and M com- 
ponents, respectively (Figure 2).

N is the number of sites, K the precision of VGP's, and A95 the 
circle of 95% confidence about the mean pole position. 
The pillow basalts did not respond coherently to alternating 
field treatment but showed good response under thermal de- 
magnetization. Two examples are shown in Figure 2. Over- 
lapping blocking temperature spectrums made it difficult to 
determine a low-temperature (200ø-400øC) component except 
in a few cases. A component that is resolved up to the Curie 
temperature of magnetite was always discernible. The two 
components have been referred to as the L and M com- 
ponents, respectively (Figure 2). 
The various components of magnetization observed in the 
Duffer Formation are listed in Table 1. They are listed first in 
situ, that is, with the rocks in their present attitude, and then 
after bedding, that is, after restoring the strata to the horizon- 
tal by simple rotation about their present strike. The structural 
corrections applied to each site are also listed in Table 1. Fig- 
ure 3 shows the effect on the M components in both the dacite 
and the pillow basalt of restoring the strata to the horizontal. 
There is a marked and dramatic improvement in grouping, 
with directions from the two localities converging to form a 
single group. The Fisher [ 1953] precision parameter increases 
from 2.45 to 30.61 for the 11 sites, which is significant at the 
99% confidence level according to the tables of McElhinny 
[1964]. This strongly suggests that these lavas have retained an 
original magnetization prior to folding about 3.0 Ga ago. If 
this is the case, this represents the oldest remanent magnet- 
ization so far observed in paleomagnetic studies. 
The L and H components are listed in Table 1 and illus- 
trated in Figure 4. After correcting the strata to the horizontal

the resulting directions do not agree either with each other or 
with any other known direction. Presumably, these are sec- 
ondary components acquired subsequent to formation. It is 
surprising that the high-temperature, high-coercivity H com- 
ponent appears to be secondary because one would expect this 
to have the greatest time stability and resistance to over- 
printing [Pullaiah et al., 1975]. However, the fact that further 
oxidation takes places during thermal demagnetization sug- 
gests that the formation of new hematite during some heating 
episode has caused the overprinting. The history of the region 
suggests that this took place either about 3.0 or 2.6 Ga ago. 
POLE POSITIONS 
Paleomagnetic pole positions calculated by combing VGP's 
for each of the M, L, and H components are summarized in 
Table 2. The L and H components are regarded as being post- 
folding and therefore derived from in situ data. The poles are 
plotted in Figure 5 along with all other pre-2.0-Ga poles from 
Australia. The Duffer Formation H component (DFH) mag- 
netization gives a pole position that lies close to that of the YE 
dykes of the Pilbara craton, dated at --2500 Ma [McElhinny 
and Embleton, 1976]. This strongly suggests that the DFH 
magnetization refers to the 2600-Ma episode in the Pilbara 
craton. The Duffer Formation M and L component, (DFM 
and DFL) magnetizations have pole positions that do not 
agree with any pre-2.0-Ga data or for that matter with any 
post-2.0-Ga results. Therefore we assume that DFM repre- 
sents the primary component at 3452 Ma in view of the fold 
test and that DFL is a component overprinted during folding 
at about 3000 Ma. This view is consistent with the simplest ex- 
trapolation of the known Precambrian apparent polar wander 
path back to 3.5 Ga (Figure 5). 
Acknowledgments. Sampling in the Marble Bar region of the Pil- 
bara craton was carried out with the assistance of R. T. Pidgeon, who 
advised on collecting localities, and N. Opdyke, who helped with 
sample collection. We gratefully acknowledge their help.
